newsitem.title: UK: Mexican peso stable in Europe but volatility seen.
newsitem.headline: Mexican peso stable in Europe but volatility seen.

text.p: Mexico's peso was stable in Europe after Sunday's congressional vote, but concerns about the government's commitment to reform and austerity were seen sparking volatility.
Preliminary results showed the ruling Insitutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) set to lose its majority in the lower house of Congress for the first time in 68 years.

"We (are) likely to get more peso volatility coming through after this. I really don't think the extent of the PRI's losses in congress were fully expected," said Richard Gray, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America.
"What's worrying is potential recriminations within the PRI over the extent of its losses, recriminations that could lead to a policy impasse or to the temptation to lean more populist," he said.

With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the PRI has won 38.23 percent, short of the 42 percent it needs to keep its decades-old majority. The National Action Party (PAN) held 27.31 percent and the PRD took 25.22 percent.
In the mid-term congressional and governors' elections, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, leader of the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), was winning comfortably in the Mexico City mayoral race.
Cardenas and the PRD's public opposition to programs like Mexico's new private pension fund system have made some investors nervous.
The PRD has also called for a larger budget deficit to boost employment, a tax on short-term foreign investments and curbs on central bank independence.

"My hunch is that it will take a bit of time for the impact of this (election) to be fully realised. But there are risks for the deficit and for fixed income markets, and this can't be good for the peso," said an emerging markets currency traded at a U.S. investment bank here.
The peso was last quoted at 7.935/945 per dollar slightly higher than 7.944/954 late on Friday but still within its 7.85 to 8.00 range since mid-March.
By winning nearly half the Mexico city vote, Cardenas was seen establishing a platform to influence political and economic agendas in the future.
Local analysts added Cardenas was likely to use the mayoral post, which has little say in national policy, to win support before the 2000 presidential vote.
Gray also said the weekend vote would pressure the government act quicker to bridge a gap between a strong export sector and a lagging domestic sector.

Economists said the election will likley be used as a confidence guage for the PRI's economic policy. During the PRI's rule since 1995 real wages have dropped about 30 percent, an economic crisis emerged and an austerity program has failed to benefit the economy's grassroots.

"Trading has been quiet so far, but it's a bit too early yet to get a full picture. And activity has been a bit distorted by the U.S. market holiday on Friday," said the emerging markets currency trader here.
U.S. markets returned from the Independence Day holiday on Monday.
